A Biblical Mystery Fiction Inspired by the King James Bible

Tears of a Father

by Michael Banks

It opens at dawn on the morning of the Rapture, with a father unaware of the world around him who misses the call. He seeks his way back to God. Then it goes back two years to the dinner table on the night the call began. This is a story of faith, redemption, mercy, and belief in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

Read Alongside the Bible

This book is a visualization of biblical prophecies. It shows how the Word can help us discern the truth and test the spirits we encounter in modern times.

This novel is written and intended to be read alongside its study guide and the Holy Bible. The goal is to use the narrative and help lead many to the true and living Word of God, which He has shared with us through the testimony and faith of His servants and prophets of old — who have helped us come to the saving knowledge of the death and resurrection and eventual return and reign of the King of Kings and Lord of Lords.

Take a journey from Genesis to Revelation in a deeply personal and exciting way. The Lord is at the door knocking. He seeks a personal, genuine, honest, and truly everlasting relationship with you. Will you let Him in to dine?

Jalen’s Piece

The Music

One piece of music runs under the whole book: Tears of a Father, a solo cello with orchestra, written by Jalen Patterson in the story.

The reader hears it in full only twice: at Jalen’s recital in Chapter 8, and the night Ezra first hears it from the flash drive in Chapter 23. Everywhere else it is an undertone: one low note through a wall, a phrase someone hums, a few seconds on a phone.

The Themes the Reader Learns to Hear

ThemeIn the musicWhat it carriesHow it reaches the page
The low lineThe opening on the open C string. It climbs a little and falls back.Grief, Angela’s illness, Ezra’s numbnessA single low note through the studio wall, held until it trembles
Every nightA three-note sigh, three times, while the harp ticks like a clockThe empty house, the couch, time passingThe same three notes through the wall; later, Mia hums them
The long noteThe high G held for seven bars, where the piece stopped for a year and a halfThe unfinished prayer; the ending nobody has heardMusic that stops in mid-air
The silenceFive seconds with everything stoppedShock, death, the morning after the RaptureThe cello stopping. “No cello.”
The climbEach phrase starts a little higher than the lastGetting up off the floor; hopeA phrase heard starting higher each time
The one noteMr. Hart’s E-flat rises to E, and C minor becomes C majorGrace; a father’s love unlockedThe smallest change in the room
The callLow C, up to G, up to C, up to the high G, then the shofarThe trumpet, the watchman’s warning, the RaptureEvery horn in the book rises in this same shape

The Piece

  • In the story: composed by Jalen Patterson; first performed at his senior recital with Lionel Hart on viola and the Coolidge High orchestra.
  • Key and length: C minor, ending in C major. About 4 minutes 40 seconds, 57 bars in 4/4, with the shofar after. The long note arrives at about 2:24.
  • Instruments: solo cello; solo viola (Mr. Hart); flute, clarinet; horns, trumpets, trombones; timpani; harp; violins I and II, violas, cellos, double basses. A distorted electric guitar and toms add weight under the final crescendo only.
  • The idea: one melody tells the whole story. It is a question in C minor; at the end it is still mourning, but no longer without hope.

The Form

SectionBarsTimeThe storyIn the music
I. Lament1–80:00The night Angela finds the lumpSolo cello alone on the open C. A soft piano enters at bar 2. The theme climbs a little and falls back.
II. The Fire9–190:38The chemo room; the clippersA restless eighth-note figure in the violas. The cello stays low and dark, then falls all the way back to the low C.
III. Every Night20–271:25The empty house; the couchThe three-note sigh repeats three times while the harp ticks strictly in time. Then a slow, dark climb begins.
IV. The Climb28–322:03The recitalThe cello climbs past every earlier peak, up to A-flat.
V. The Long Note33–392:24The note he could never get pastThe high G held for seven bars. The orchestra murmurs beneath it; time stretches wider and wider.
The Silenceend of 392:58The breathEverything stops for about five seconds.
VI. The Return40–453:03Starting againThe cello alone, low and soft and slow. Strings and piano enter at bar 42, barely there.
VII. The Slow Build46–513:25Climbing backEach phrase starts higher. Violins join an octave above, then horns, trombones, winds and harp.
VIII. The Final Crescendo52–534:03“And then it broke open”The cello’s high C over an A-flat major chord. Full orchestra, guitar swell, crash and timpani.
IX. The Answer54–574:13A father’s love, unlockedThe shofar call. The line sinks to a low C, then breaks upward the way a ram’s horn does, C to G to C, landing on a high G, the highest note in the piece.

The Ending

The piece ends with the orchestra’s cry. The cello holds its high G two seconds longer and does not fade; it keeps the note to the very end with a slow, wide vibrato. Out of nothing the whole orchestra swells on an A-flat major chord, leans on F minor, and breaks open into C major at full voice. A solo violin leads the cry up a step with each chord to the high G. A soft ticking begins slowly and speeds up until it is almost a flutter, stopping exactly on the C major. The harp enters with a sweep and sings the opening grief theme, high and clear, in C major. The shofar sounds after a short silence.

Mr. Hart’s viola

The cello leads the whole piece. Beneath it, Jalen’s teacher plays a small solo viola part, kept quiet on purpose: “This is your piece. I’m just the floor under it.” He holds one long, soft note under each chord, and falls silent for the long note and the cello’s return, which belong to Jalen alone. In the last two bars he holds an E-flat under the cello’s C (C minor), then moves that one note up to E (C major). That glimmer is the only moment the viola is truly heard.

Sheet Music Themes

Written as note names until a full engraved score exists.

The grief theme, solo cello, from the open C string:

C (held) — G, A♭, B♭ — C (held), D — E♭, D, C — B♭, A♭ — G (held) — A♭, G, F, E♭ — D, C

The return, in its plainest form:

C, E♭, D — C (held), G — A♭, C, E♭ — D (held)

The climb, two bars at a time, each phrase starting a little higher:

E♭, G, A♭ — G, F — A♭, C, E♭ — D — E♭, F, G — A♭, G — F, E♭, D — E♭, F, G, B♭ — high C (held)

The answer: the line falls G, F, E♭, D to a held middle C. Under it, the viola holds E♭ (C minor), then moves it up to E (C major). Then the call: low C, G, C, high G, held. Then the shofar.

The People

Meet the Cast

The people you will hear, and the people you will meet in the pages. Each one is paired with a verse from the King James Bible that speaks to who they are.

The Pattersons

Ezra Patterson

44, a builder and a father

A skilled carpenter with callused hands and a quiet heart, doing his best to hold a family together. He tells part of this story himself.

“Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it.”

Ezra 7:10

In the book “And his father saw him a great way off and ran to him, and the boy never got to finish the speech. Did you ever notice that? He got halfway through it, and his father was already shouting for the robe and the ring and the shoes.”

Angela Patterson

42, Ezra's wife

A third-grade teacher with a bright laugh, a purple scarf, and a black notebook she fills late at night at the dinner table.

“She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.”

Proverbs 31:26

In the book “It's all in here. All of it. Just like He said it would be.”

Jalen Patterson

19, their son

A gifted young cellist and composer who says the most when he is playing and the least when he is talking.

“Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.”

Psalm 33:3

In the book “I'm dedicating this to someone who isn't here right now.”

Mia Patterson

6, their daughter

Small, sweet and watchful. She draws what she sees and asks the questions the grown-ups are afraid of.

“Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.”

Matthew 19:14

In the book “I heard you yelling. So I waited till you stopped.”

Loretta Patterson

Ezra's mother

Small, straight-backed, an alto in the same church choir for fifty years. She has prayed for her son every morning of his life.

“The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.”

James 5:16

In the book “He made you think the God he preached about was the same as the man he was.”

Deacon Calvin Patterson

Ezra's late father

A deacon and country preacher whose name still carries weight at the church, and whose shadow still falls across his son.

“For the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”

1 Samuel 16:7

In the book “I quoted, “Wives, submit,” to your mother and left out the next verse. I quoted, “Children, obey,” to you and left out, “Fathers, provoke not.” I used His Word like a strap.”

The Watchmen

Kambria Elliott

42, a forensic scientist

A CDC scientist raised by a Baltimore grandmother who read her Daniel at the kitchen table. Angela's closest friend, and the first to stay awake.

“I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me.”

Habakkuk 2:1

In the book “Ezra, I don't think there's time to wait until you're ready. Please. Open it. Tonight. Before you go wherever you're going.”

Walt Simmons

74, a retired typesetter

Lives across the street. Forty years of setting headlines in lead type taught him to get every word right, and he keeps a ledger of the news with a verse beside each entry.

“Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.”

Habakkuk 2:2

In the book “Trembling won't save you either. You have to come to Him. Not to the book about Him. To Him.”

Pastor Xavier Grant

61, Angela's pastor

A gentle, gray-haired man with a fountain pen and a pocket calendar, who answers every question plainly, even the hard ones.

“Speaking the truth in love.”

Ephesians 4:15

In the book “I've sat at a lot of deathbeds. I've never seen anybody less sick than that woman in there. Her body is failing. But her soul is the healthiest thing in this house.”

Ezra's World

Elijah Brooks

44, Ezra's oldest friend

Third stool from the wall, every night. The funniest man in the neighborhood, and, Ezra has long suspected, the saddest.

“Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.”

Proverbs 14:13

In the book “Every night of my life, even at the bar, even when I was laughing, there was something, way down, calling.”

Trent Walker

Ezra's apprentice

Quick, sharp and good with his hands, he quotes Scripture with a smirk and misses nothing.

“Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only.”

James 1:22

In the book “I know exactly what it's saying. I'm just choosing the fun half.”

Celeste Moore

A hospital volunteer

Red-haired, warm, and always ready with a kind word for the family in the waiting room.

“The lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil.”

Proverbs 5:3

In the book “Everything that breaks is waiting to be repaired. That's the whole secret. Nobody has to die for you. You climb.”

Jalen's Music

Lionel Hart

A retired violist

Thirty-one years with the Capital Philharmonic. He fixed Jalen's bow hold without a word and offered to teach him for nothing.

“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.”

Proverbs 22:6

In the book “This is your piece. I'm just the floor under it.”

Dr. Evelyn Shaw

Director, Young Artists Program

Slight and tidy, in a charcoal suit, with reading glasses on a chain. She listens harder than anyone else in the room.

“A man's gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men.”

Proverbs 18:16

In the book “Lionel Hart has been telling me about you for three years. I came to find out if he was exaggerating. He wasn't.”

The Powers

Adrian Crowe

An international statesman

Smooth, generous and easy in every room. He never raises his voice, and the world has begun to hang on his every word.

“For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them.”

1 Thessalonians 5:3

In the book “Peace. Order. Safety. That is my promise to you. I intend to keep it.”

In Loving Memory

Dedication

This book is dedicated to Theresa Banks, my beloved wife, whose beautiful soul shone brightly through twenty-one years of fighting breast cancer with faith, courage, and grace. Until I see you again.

For Theresa Banks,

my beloved wife, whose beautiful soul shone brightly through twenty-one years of fighting breast cancer with faith, courage, and grace. She went home to be with the Lord on March 9, 2020.

Until I see you again.
